en.greeting: Hi! Today is about English that doesn't mean exactly what it says: metaphors, puns and cultural references. By the end, you'll get the joke, and you'll be able to say why it's funny.

steps.title: Metaphor and simile
steps.text: Quick recap, then the system behind a lot of idioms.
steps.body:
You know idioms are fixed phrases you can't translate word by word, and that words carry a feeling (connotation). Behind many idioms is **figurative language**: words used for a picture.

A **simile** compares with **like** or **as ... as**: *as busy as a bee*. A **metaphor** says one thing **is** another: *This office is a zoo.* Indonesian has both: *bagai pinang dibelah dua* ≈ **like two peas in a pod** (same idea, different picture). Careful: *as clear as mud* is ironic = not clear at all.

pairs.en: like a fish out of water
like two peas in a pod

steps.title: Metaphors English lives by
steps.text: Some metaphors are so common that native speakers don't notice them. They come in families.
steps.body: **Time is money:** spend, save, waste, invest time (Indonesian says *buang waktu* too). **Argument is war:** attack a position, defend a claim, shoot down an idea, win an argument. **Ideas are food:** a half-baked plan (setengah matang), food for thought (bahan renungan), digest a report (mencerna).

examples.en: Let's not waste time on the details: the client wants a decision today.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.text: Rina presented her plan for a four-day work week to the board of her startup in Bandung. Afterwards she messages a friend: 'The board shot down my proposal in five minutes.'

options: The board quickly and firmly rejected it.
The board approved it after a short discussion.
The board asked her to shorten it to five minutes.
question.explanation: **shoot down** comes from the **argument is war** family: the idea is a plane, and shooting it down destroys it. So the board rejected it, fast and firmly. *Five minutes* is how long that took, not a new length for her talk.

steps.title: Four more figures of speech
steps.text: English also makes things human, makes them bigger or smaller, or names them through a neighbour.
steps.body:
**Personification** (benda seperti manusia): *The economy is recovering. My laptop died.*
**Hyperbole** (dilebih-lebihkan): *I've told you a million times.*
**Understatement** (dikecilkan), very British: *That's not ideal* about a flood = it's a disaster; *not bad* = quite good. Don't take it literally!
**Metonymy** (disebut lewat hal yang dekat): *The White House said...* = the US president's team. Indonesian news does it too: *Istana*, *Senayan* (= DPR).

steps.title: Indonesian expressions: twins and traps
steps.text: Now the trap that catches even advanced learners: translating Indonesian figurative expressions word for word.
steps.body:
Some are **twins**: *kambing hitam* = **a scapegoat** (a lucky match; not *a black sheep*). Some are **cousins**, same idea with another picture: *kutu buku* = **a bookworm**, *lintah darat* = **a loan shark**. Many are **traps**: *panjang tangan* isn't 'long-handed' but **light-fingered**; *makan hati* isn't 'eat liver' (say *It really gets to me*).

And keep **one picture** per sentence: *nip it in the bud before it snowballs*, not *... snowballs out of the water* (garden + snow + sea = a **mixed metaphor**).

steps.title: Your turn
steps.text: Sari's cousin works in Melbourne and has a new boyfriend. Sari hears that he's dating three other women at the same time. In Indonesian she'd say: Dia itu buaya darat.

question.prompt: Which sentence should Sari write to her cousin in English?
options: He's a land crocodile, so be careful.
He's a bit of a player, so be careful.
He's a bit of a loan shark, so be careful.
question.explanation: *buaya darat* → **a player** (or *a womaniser*, US *womanizer*): a man who dates many women and isn't serious. 'A land crocodile' is a word-for-word translation English speakers won't understand. **A loan shark** is *lintah darat*: another animal, another meaning.

steps.title: Puns: one word, two meanings
steps.text: Now humour. Many English jokes are puns: think of plesetan, or jokes bapak-bapak. English calls the cheesy kind dad jokes.
steps.body:
A **pun** uses a word with **two meanings**, or two words that **sound the same** (homophones: *two / too*). The **set-up** makes you think of one meaning; the **punchline** (kalimat penutup) switches to the other.

*I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.* You hear 'lost interest' as kehilangan minat, then remember banks pay **interest** (bunga bank). Both fit: that's the joke. The usual reaction is a groan and a smile. To get a pun, ask: **which word works both ways?**

steps.title: Get the joke
steps.text: At lunch, Budi tells this joke: 'My mechanic quit last week. He said he was exhausted.' Everyone groans and laughs.

question.prompt: Which word carries the double meaning?
options: mechanic
quit
exhausted
question.explanation: **exhausted** = very tired, and an **exhaust** (knalpot) is part of a car, which is a mechanic's work. It sounds like a normal complaint about being tired, then the car meaning pops up: that's the pun. *quit* and *mechanic* have only one meaning here.

steps.title: Cultural references (allusions)
steps.text: Last: names and stories English speakers expect you to know.
steps.body: An **allusion** is a short reference to a famous story, used without explanation. Calling someone *Malin Kundang* works in Indonesian; English draws on Greek myths, the Bible, fairy tales and novels. *Achilles' heel* (said a-KIL-iiz): the hero could only be hurt on his heel. *A Trojan horse*: soldiers hidden in a wooden 'gift'. *A Catch-22* (a 1961 novel): rules that trap you in a circle. *Big Brother* (Orwell's novel *1984*): a power that watches everyone. *Sherlock* (the detective) is often used sarcastically.

pairs.id: masalah besar yang semua orang hindari

steps.title: Your turn
steps.text: Dimas and Rina are driving to a client in Bogor. The engine stops, and the fuel light has been on for 30 kilometres. Dimas looks at the dashboard and says, 'I think we've run out of fuel.' Rina replies: 'No kidding, Sherlock.'

options: She's impressed by his clever detective work.
She's teasing him for saying something obvious.
She thinks he's lying about the fuel.
question.explanation: Sherlock Holmes is the famous detective, so calling someone **Sherlock** after an obvious 'discovery' is **sarcasm**: the opposite of praise. The fuel light was on for 30 km, so everyone already knew. Rina doesn't think he's lying; she's teasing him.

id.greeting: Hai! Hari ini kita belajar bahasa Inggris yang artinya tidak persis seperti kata-katanya: metafora, pun dan referensi budaya. Di akhir pelajaran, kamu akan menangkap leluconnya, dan bisa menjelaskan kenapa lucu.

steps.title: Metafora dan simile
steps.text: Ulasan singkat dulu, lalu sistem di balik banyak idiom.
steps.body:
Kamu sudah tahu idiom adalah frasa tetap yang tak bisa diterjemahkan kata per kata, dan kata membawa 'rasa' (konotasi). Di balik banyak idiom ada **bahasa kiasan**: kata yang dipakai untuk sebuah gambaran.

**Simile** (perumpamaan) membandingkan dengan **like** atau **as ... as**: *as busy as a bee*. **Metafora** menyatakan sesuatu **adalah** hal lain: *This office is a zoo.* Bahasa Indonesia punya keduanya: *bagai pinang dibelah dua* ≈ **like two peas in a pod** (idenya sama, gambarannya beda). Hati-hati: *as clear as mud* itu ironis = sama sekali tidak jelas.

pairs.en: like a fish out of water
like two peas in a pod

steps.title: Metafora sehari-hari bahasa Inggris
steps.text: Ada metafora yang begitu umum sampai penutur asli tidak menyadarinya. Metafora ini datang dalam 'keluarga'.
steps.body: **Time is money (waktu adalah uang):** spend, save, waste, invest time (bahasa Indonesia juga bilang *buang waktu*). **Argument is war (berdebat itu berperang):** attack a position, defend a claim, shoot down an idea, win an argument. **Ideas are food (ide itu makanan):** a half-baked plan (setengah matang), food for thought (bahan renungan), digest a report (mencerna).

steps.title: Giliranmu
steps.text: Rina mempresentasikan rencana empat hari kerja seminggu kepada dewan direksi startup-nya di Bandung. Setelah itu dia mengirim pesan ke temannya: 'The board shot down my proposal in five minutes.'

question.prompt: Apa yang terjadi pada usulan Rina?
options: The board quickly and firmly rejected it.
The board approved it after a short discussion.
The board asked her to shorten it to five minutes.
question.explanation: **shoot down** berasal dari keluarga **argument is war**: idenya ibarat pesawat, dan menembaknya jatuh berarti menghancurkannya. Jadi dewan direksi menolaknya dengan cepat dan tegas. *Five minutes* adalah lama penolakannya, bukan durasi baru untuk presentasinya.
displayOptions: Dewan memintanya mempersingkat usulan menjadi lima menit.

steps.title: Empat majas lainnya
steps.text: Bahasa Inggris juga membuat benda seperti manusia, membesar-besarkan atau mengecilkan, atau menyebut sesuatu lewat 'tetangganya'.
steps.body:
**Personifikasi** (benda seperti manusia): *The economy is recovering. My laptop died.*
**Hiperbola** (dilebih-lebihkan): *I've told you a million times.*
**Understatement** (dikecilkan), sangat British: *That's not ideal* tentang banjir = sebenarnya bencana; *not bad* = cukup bagus. Jangan diartikan harfiah!
**Metonimi** (disebut lewat hal yang dekat): *The White House said...* = tim Presiden AS. Berita Indonesia juga begitu: *Istana*, *Senayan* (= DPR).

steps.title: Ungkapan Indonesia: kembar dan jebakan
steps.text: Sekarang jebakan yang menjerat pelajar tingkat lanjut sekalipun: menerjemahkan ungkapan kiasan Indonesia kata per kata.
steps.body:
Ada yang **kembar**: *kambing hitam* = **a scapegoat** (kebetulan cocok; bukan *a black sheep*). Ada yang **sepupu**, idenya sama dengan gambaran lain: *kutu buku* = **a bookworm**, *lintah darat* = **a loan shark**. Banyak yang **jebakan**: *panjang tangan* bukan 'long-handed' tapi **light-fingered**; *makan hati* bukan 'eat liver' (katakan *It really gets to me*).

Dan pakai **satu gambaran** per kalimat: *nip it in the bud before it snowballs*, bukan *... snowballs out of the water* (kebun + salju + laut = **mixed metaphor**, metafora campur aduk).

steps.title: Giliranmu
steps.text: Sepupu Sari bekerja di Melbourne dan punya pacar baru. Sari dengar pacarnya itu sedang berkencan dengan tiga perempuan lain sekaligus. Dalam bahasa Indonesia dia akan bilang: Dia itu buaya darat.

question.prompt: Kalimat bahasa Inggris mana yang sebaiknya Sari tulis untuk sepupunya?
options: He's a land crocodile, so be careful.
He's a bit of a player, so be careful.
He's a bit of a loan shark, so be careful.
question.explanation: *buaya darat* → **a player** (atau *a womaniser*, ejaan AS *womanizer*): laki-laki yang mengencani banyak perempuan dan tidak serius. 'A land crocodile' adalah terjemahan kata per kata yang tidak akan dipahami penutur bahasa Inggris. **A loan shark** itu *lintah darat*: hewan lain, arti lain.

steps.title: Pun: satu kata, dua arti
steps.text: Sekarang humor. Banyak lelucon bahasa Inggris berupa pun: bayangkan plesetan, atau jokes bapak-bapak. Bahasa Inggris menyebut versi yang garing dad jokes.
steps.body:
**Pun** memakai kata dengan **dua arti**, atau dua kata yang **bunyinya sama** (homofon: *two / too*). **Set-up** (bagian awal) membuatmu memikirkan satu arti; **punchline** (kalimat penutup) berbelok ke arti yang lain.

*I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.* Kamu mendengar 'lost interest' sebagai kehilangan minat, lalu ingat bahwa bank memberi **interest** (bunga bank). Dua-duanya cocok: itulah leluconnya. Reaksi biasanya mengeluh 'aduh...' sambil tersenyum. Untuk menangkap pun, tanyakan: **kata mana yang berlaku dua arah?**

steps.title: Tangkap leluconnya
steps.text: Saat makan siang, Budi menceritakan lelucon ini: 'My mechanic quit last week. He said he was exhausted.' Semua orang mengeluh 'aduh...' lalu tertawa.

question.prompt: Kata mana yang membawa makna ganda?
options: mechanic
quit
exhausted
question.explanation: **exhausted** = sangat lelah, dan **exhaust** (knalpot) adalah bagian mobil, yang merupakan pekerjaan montir. Kalimatnya terdengar seperti keluhan biasa soal capek, lalu arti mobilnya muncul: itulah pun-nya. *quit* dan *mechanic* hanya punya satu arti di sini.

steps.title: Referensi budaya (alusi)
steps.text: Terakhir: nama dan cerita yang dianggap sudah kamu kenal oleh penutur bahasa Inggris.
steps.body: **Alusi** adalah rujukan singkat ke cerita terkenal, dipakai tanpa penjelasan. Menyebut seseorang *Malin Kundang* langsung dipahami dalam bahasa Indonesia; bahasa Inggris mengambil dari mitos Yunani, Alkitab, dongeng dan novel. *Achilles' heel* (dibaca a-KIL-iiz): sang pahlawan hanya bisa dilukai di tumitnya. *A Trojan horse*: tentara yang disembunyikan dalam 'hadiah' kuda kayu. *A Catch-22* (novel 1961): aturan yang menjebak dalam lingkaran. *Big Brother* (novel Orwell, *1984*): penguasa yang mengawasi semua orang. *Sherlock* (sang detektif) sering dipakai untuk menyindir.

steps.title: Giliranmu
steps.text: Dimas dan Rina menyetir ke kantor klien di Bogor. Mesinnya mati, dan lampu bensin sudah menyala sejak 30 kilometer tadi. Dimas melihat dasbor dan berkata, 'I think we've run out of fuel.' Rina menjawab: 'No kidding, Sherlock.'

options: She's impressed by his clever detective work.
She's teasing him for saying something obvious.
She thinks he's lying about the fuel.
question.explanation: Sherlock Holmes adalah detektif terkenal, jadi memanggil seseorang **Sherlock** setelah 'penemuan' yang sudah jelas adalah **sarkasme**: kebalikan dari pujian. Lampu bensin sudah menyala 30 km, jadi semua orang sudah tahu. Rina tidak menganggap Dimas berbohong; dia sedang meledeknya.
displayOptions: Dia menyindirnya karena mengatakan hal yang sudah jelas.
Dia menganggapnya berbohong soal bahan bakar.
